issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising revisional jurisdiction in a rent-control matter cannot reappreciate evidence and reverse supported findings of fact made by the first appellate authority unless those findings are not according to law.
material_facts: The first appellate court considered the evidence and made findings that the landlord-tenant relationship existed and that rent had been willfully unpaid.
The High Court reappreciated the evidence and reversed the first appellate court’s factual findings without identifying a jurisdictional error or other legal defect in them.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded the limits of its revisional jurisdiction; its order was set aside and the first appellate court’s judgment was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under the principle stated by the Constitution Bench in Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Dilbahar Singh, (2014) 9 SCC 78, a rent-control revisional court may examine whether a finding is according to law, including whether it is perverse, unsupported by evidence, based on disregard or misreading of material evidence, or procedurally illegal. It may not reassess evidence merely to reach a different factual view as if hearing a first appeal.

rule.if: rent_control_revision and first_appellate_findings_supported_by_evidence and not jurisdictional_or_legal_error_in_findings and high_court_reassessed_evidence

predicates.rent_control_revision: The proceeding before the High Court was a revision arising from a rent-control matter.
predicates.first_appellate_findings_supported_by_ev: The first appellate authority considered the evidence and made factual findings supported by that evidence.
predicates.jurisdictional_or_legal_error_in_finding: The first appellate authority’s findings contained a jurisdictional or other legal error.
predicates.high_court_reassessed_evidence: The High Court reappreciated the evidence to reach a different factual view.
predicates.high_court_revision_interference_imprope: The High Court’s interference with the first appellate findings exceeded the proper limits of revisional review.

issues.definition: When a rent-control revision concerns supported first-appellate findings and those findings contain no jurisdictional or legal error, reappreciating the evidence to reach a different factual view makes the High Court’s interference improper.

issues.legal_issue: In a rent-control eviction proceeding, evidence establishing the landlord’s entitlement to control the premises and the tenant’s willful rent default can sustain eviction where the tenant fails to prove a claim that the apparent sale was only a mortgage.
material_facts: The landlords relied on a sale deed in favour of their predecessors and evidence of the occupants’ tenancy under the landlords’ predecessors.
The occupants alleged that the sale was a mortgage and that their predecessors remained the owners, but they adduced no documentary or oral evidence to prove that defence.
The first appellate court found that the landlord-tenant relationship was established and that rent had been willfully unpaid; the Supreme Court found no jurisdictional error in those findings.
issues.conclusion: The evidence was sufficient to maintain the eviction petition, and the first appellate court was justified in allowing it on the grounds of the established landlord-tenant relationship and willful default.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10 of the A.P. Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, governed the eviction petition. In a rent-control landlord-tenant dispute, ownership is relative to the context and may be established by showing a legal entitlement to evict the tenant and retain control of the premises; it need not meet the standard applicable in a title suit (Sheela v. Firm Prahlad Rai Prem Prakash, (2002) 3 SCC 375). The party asserting that an apparent sale was actually a mortgage bears the burden of proving that defence. Supported first-appellate findings are not open to reversal in revision absent a jurisdictional or legal error, as explained in Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Dilbahar Singh, (2014) 9 SCC 78.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and landlord_entitlement_supported_by_evidence and tenant_relationship_established and tenant_failed_to_prove_sale_was_mortgage and willful_rent_default_found

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding sought eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.landlord_entitlement_supported_by_eviden: The claimant produced evidence sufficient in the rent-control proceeding to establish a legal entitlement to control the premises and seek eviction.
predicates.tenant_relationship_established: The evidence established that the occupant held the premises as a tenant of the claimant or the claimant’s predecessor.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_prove_sale_was_mortgage: The tenant asserted that an apparent sale was only a mortgage but did not prove that assertion.
predicates.willful_rent_default_found: The fact-finder determined that the tenant willfully failed to pay rent.

issues.definition: In a rent-control eviction proceeding, supported evidence of the claimant’s entitlement and the tenancy, together with an unproven mortgage defence and a finding of willful rent default, means eviction is justified.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot raise new factual grounds for the first time in an appeal when those grounds were not pleaded or raised during the earlier proceedings.
material_facts: The occupants argued in the Supreme Court that there had been an encroachment and that a document was inadmissible.
Neither contention had been raised in the written statement before the Rent Controller or urged at any earlier stage.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the contentions because they were factual submissions raised for the first time in the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to permit factual submissions to be raised for the first time on appeal when they had not been pleaded before the original decision-maker or urged during the earlier proceedings.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The matter was being considered in an appellate proceeding.
predicates.factual_ground_not_pleaded_below: The factual ground was not included in the party’s pleading before the original decision-maker.
predicates.factual_ground_not_raised_at_earlier_sta: The factual ground was not urged at any earlier stage of the proceedings.
predicates.new_factual_ground_not_considered: The court does not consider the factual ground first advanced on appeal.

issues.definition: In an appeal, a factual ground that was neither pleaded below nor raised earlier is not considered when advanced for the first time.
